intro.html: Anger comes in many sizes and flavors. Some words tell how strong it is (vexed is mild; livid and irate are hot). Some tell why (indignant anger is about unfairness). Some describe a temper rather than a moment (irascible, petulant). And some name anger that has hardened over time into ill will (rancor, animosity, enmity).
Latin ira means anger: you can hear it in irate and irascible. A moment of anger: irate, livid, wrath. A temper: irascible, petulant. Long-lasting ill will: rancor, animosity, enmity.

words.ex: Ivy was {indignant} when she was blamed for the vase the cat had broken.
words.ctx: The players were {indignant}, not because they lost, but because the referee had ignored three clear fouls against their goalie.
words.etym: From Latin indignari, “to consider unworthy, be angry at”: in- (not) + dignus (worthy).
words.note: Indignant anger is about unfairness, not just any annoyance.

mn.text: Ivy is blamed for the broken vase she never touched. “I did NOT!” she cries, angry at the unfairness. She is {indignant}.

scene.alt: A girl wrongly blamed for a broken vase protests angrily while the cat who did it sneaks away.

words.ex: Usually the calmest man on the street, Mr. Lee was {irate} when he found his garden trampled.
words.ctx: After waiting four hours on the runway with no food or news, the passengers were {irate}, and several of them shouted at the crew.

mn.text: Rex finds his soup stone cold, turns red and shouts, “I rate this place zero stars!” He is {irate}.

scene.alt: A furious customer shouts at a worried waiter holding a bowl of soup.

words.ex: Dad was {livid} when he saw the scratch on his new car.
words.ctx: The coach was not merely annoyed but {livid}; his face turned red, and he kicked the water bucket across the field after the third missed goal.
words.etym: From Latin lividus, “bluish, black and blue,” the color of a bruise; the sense “furious” came much later.
words.note: In everyday use livid means furious. Its old meaning, bluish-gray like a bruise, still shows up in older books.

mn.text: When the goat eats his prize pie, Farmer Gus is so furious he flips his lid. He is {livid}.

scene.alt: A furious old farmer shouts at a happy goat that has eaten his pie.

words.ex: The {irascible} old cat hissed at anyone who came near its basket.
words.ctx: The {irascible} editor would fly into a rage over a single misplaced comma, so new writers checked their work three times before handing it in.
words.etym: From Latin irascibilis, from irasci, “to grow angry,” from ira (anger).

mn.cue: IRA-SCIBLE: IRA flares up at everything
mn.text: Old Ira snaps at the mail carrier, the wind and even the birds; the smallest thing sets him off. Ira is {irascible}.

scene.alt: A cranky man named Ira yells at a chirping bird while the startled mail carrier looks on.

words.ex: Told to turn off his game, the {petulant} boy pouted, sulked and stomped up the stairs.
words.ctx: Instead of congratulating the winner, the {petulant} runner-up stomped off the court, refused to shake hands and sulked on the bus all the way home.

mn.cue: PET-ulant: sulks like a spoiled PET
mn.text: When he doesn’t get a second treat, Biscuit the puppy turns his back and sulks. What a {petulant} pet!

scene.alt: A puppy turns away and sulks because the girl will give him only one treat.

words.ex: The squeaky door {vexed} Grandpa all winter.
words.ctx: The math problem {vexed} the whole class for a week; every answer they tried came out a little wrong, and no one could see why.

mn.text: Tap, tap, tap: every morning at five, a crow pecks at Grandpa’s window. Those pecks {vex} him no end.

scene.alt: A grumpy grandfather sits up in bed while a crow taps at his window at dawn.

words.ex: The cat’s {wrath} was terrible when it was lifted into the bathtub.
words.ctx: Fearing the {wrath} of the head chef, the cooks scrubbed every pot until it shone before she came back from her break.

mn.text: Try to give the cat a bath and you will see true {wrath}: hissing, splashing, fur-on-end fury.

labels.text: WRATH = a cat in a BATH

scene.alt: A furious cat leaps hissing out of a bucket of bath water while a boy holding soap looks shocked.

words.def: bitter resentment that lasts a long time
words.ex: Years after the contest, he still spoke of the judges with {rancor}, a bitterness that never faded.
words.ctx: Though the two neighbors had settled the fence dispute in court long ago, the {rancor} between them lingered, and they still refused to wave to each other.
words.etym: From Latin rancor, “rankness, a grudge,” related to rancidus (stinking), the source of rancid.

mn.cue: r-ANCHOR: a grudge you drag for years
mn.text: Thirty years after losing the pie contest, Victor still drags his grudge around like a heavy anchor. Bitter resentment that lasts that long is {rancor}.

scene.alt: A grumpy man drags a heavy anchor on a chain, still brooding over an old grudge.

words.ex: There was no {animosity} between the rivals; they shook hands after every match.
words.ctx: The {animosity} between the two clubs ran so deep that the league scheduled their games on different days to keep the fans apart.

roots.means: the quality of being full of

words.etym: From Latin animositas, “boldness, high spirit,” from animus (spirit, mind); the sense of ill will came later.

mn.text: The cat and the dog next door hiss and growl at each other across the fence every single day. Their {animosity} is plain to see.

scene.alt: An angry dog and an angry cat glare at each other across a garden fence.

words.ex: The {enmity} between the two families lasted three generations.
words.ctx: The old {enmity} between the river towns finally ended when a flood forced them to work side by side, and they found they liked each other.
words.etym: From Old French enemistie, from Latin inimicus, “enemy”: in- (not) + amicus (friend).

mn.text: The kings of the two castles have been enemies for a hundred years, and neither will even nod to the other. Their {enmity} never fades.

scene.alt: Two kings with crossed arms glare at each other from opposite sides, each beside his own flag.

head: kind of anger
words
rows: a flash of anger right now
after.cap: Sort the words by what kind of anger they name.

after.html: Livid first meant bluish-gray, the color of a bruise. Most readers now take it to mean furious, and that is the sense tests expect; the color sense survives in older writing (a livid sky).

choices: being punished for something a sibling did
stubbing a toe on a chair
waking up on a rainy day
items.why: Indignant anger is about unfairness: being punished for someone else’s act is unfair.

items.q: In “Her face was livid with rage,” livid most nearly means…
items.why: In everyday use livid means furious. (Its old color sense, bluish-gray, would not fit “with rage.”)

items.q: Which word names anger that has lasted a long time?
items.why: Rancor is bitter resentment that lingers for years; irate and vex describe anger in the moment, and petulant describes a sulky temper.

items.q: True or false: an irascible person stays calm no matter what.
items.why: False. Irascible comes from Latin ira, “anger”: an irascible person is easily angered.
